labels.kjvtr: How the King James Bible translates it
labels.credit: Strong’s Concordance (1890) · STEPBible.org lexicons and tagged texts (CC BY 4.0)

G373.use: Used about 12 times in the New Testament, in 8 books — first in Matthew 11:28; most often in Philemon (2), Revelation (2) and Matthew (2).
senses: To give someone a break from labour, to give rest or refresh them, as in Matthew 11:28.
To refresh someone's heart or spirit, as Paul says believers did for him and for others.
To take rest or enjoy rest oneself, whether a short pause from work or the rest of those who die in the Lord.
Of God's Spirit, to rest upon a person, as in 1 Peter 4:14.
G373.note: The word is built from 'up' plus 'stop', picturing a pause that refreshes. In the Greek Old Testament it most often translates the Hebrew verb for 'to rest' (nuach).

H7673.use: Used about 71 times in the Old Testament, in 19 books — first in Genesis 2:2; most often in Ezekiel (13), Isaiah (10) and Exodus (7).
senses: To cease or stop, to come to an end.
To rest or stop working, as God did on the seventh day in Genesis 2:2.
To keep or observe the sabbath.
To make something stop: to put an end to it, remove it, or cause it to fail.
H7673.note: The basic idea is stopping rather than relaxing. The word 'sabbath' comes from this verb, so the sabbath is literally a 'stopping' day.

G1680.use: Used about 54 times in the New Testament, in 15 books — first in Acts 2:26; most often in Romans (13), Acts (8) and Hebrews (5).
senses: Expectation of something good; in the New Testament it is always a hopeful, not fearful, expectation.
Religious hope, such as Israel's hope for the Messiah or the Christian hope of eternal life, as in Titus 3:7.
The person or thing that is the ground of hope, as when Christ is called 'our hope' in 1 Timothy 1:1.
The thing hoped for itself, such as 'the hope laid up for you in heaven' in Colossians 1:5.
G1680.note: Romans uses this word more than any other book, including 'we are saved in hope' (Romans 8:24) and 'the God of hope' (Romans 15:13). It is also one of the three that 'abide' in 1 Corinthians 13:13.

H8615.use: Used about 34 times in the Old Testament, in 10 books — first in Joshua 2:18; most often in Job (13), Proverbs (8) and Psalms (3).
senses: Literally, a cord or line, something that attaches or holds on.
Hope or expectation, a looking forward to what is to come.
The ground or reason for hope.
The thing hoped for, or the final outcome someone looks toward.
H8615.note: Its first use, in Joshua 2:18, is the literal 'line of scarlet thread' Rahab tied in her window. The same word is translated 'hope' elsewhere, so the cord and the hope share one Hebrew term.

G26.use: Used about 116 times in the New Testament, in 24 books — first in Matthew 24:12; most often in 1 John (18), 1 Corinthians (14) and Ephesians (10).
senses: Love, goodwill and esteem between people, as in John 13:35.
People's love toward God, as in 1 John 2:5.
God's love for people, as in Romans 5:8, and Christ's love for people, as in Romans 8:35.
In the plural, 'love feasts', the shared meals of early believers mentioned in Jude 12.
G26.note: Scholars find almost no clear examples of this noun outside the Bible and church writings, so the New Testament gave it its distinctive weight. First John uses it more than any other book.

H160.use: Used about 38 times in the Old Testament, in 14 books — first in Genesis 29:20; most often in Song of Solomon (11), Proverbs (5) and Jeremiah (3).
senses: Human love of one person for another, including friendship.
Love between a man and a woman, including romantic and sexual desire.
God's love for his people.
Strong's notes it can describe affection in a bad sense as well as a good one.
H160.note: Its first use is Genesis 29:20, where Jacob's seven years of work for Rachel seemed only a few days because of his love for her. The Song of Solomon uses it more than any other book.

G3982.use: Used about 55 times in the New Testament, in 14 books — first in Matthew 27:20; most often in Acts (17), Philippians (6) and Romans (5).
senses: To persuade, win over or prevail upon someone, as Paul did in the synagogues in Acts 18:4.
To trust or be confident, as in 'being confident of this very thing' in Philippians 1:6.
To be persuaded or convinced, as in Romans 8:38, 'I am persuaded that neither death nor life...'.
To listen to and obey someone, as in Hebrews 13:17.
G3982.note: The word moves from 'persuading' to 'being persuaded' to 'trusting': one fully persuaded is confident. In the Greek Old Testament it mainly translates the Hebrew batach, 'to trust'.

H982.use: Used about 120 times in the Old Testament, in 16 books — first in Deuteronomy 28:52; most often in Psalms (46), Isaiah (20) and Jeremiah (16).
senses: To trust in, rely on, or put confidence in someone or something.
To be confident, bold, and secure.
To make someone trust, or to make them feel secure.
To feel safe in a careless or complacent way, which the KJV sometimes renders 'careless'.
H982.note: Strong's suggests the root picture is taking refuge, hiding somewhere safe. The Psalms use it more than any other book, 46 times.

G4336.use: Used about 87 times in the New Testament, in 15 books — first in Matthew 5:44; most often in Luke (19), Acts (16) and Matthew (16).
senses: To pray, always meaning prayer addressed to God.
To pray for others, including enemies, as in Matthew 5:44.
To ask in prayer for a specific thing to happen, as in Mark 13:18.
To pray in or by the Spirit, as in Ephesians 6:18.
G4336.note: Luke uses this word more than any other book and often shows Jesus praying at key moments, such as his baptism (Luke 3:21) and before choosing the twelve (Luke 6:12).

H6419.use: Used about 84 times in the Old Testament, in 18 books — first in Genesis 20:7; most often in 2 Chronicles (14), 1 Samuel (11) and Jeremiah (10).
senses: To step in or intervene between parties.
To mediate or act as judge.
To intercede on behalf of someone else.
To pray.
H6419.note: Its first use is Genesis 20:7, where God says Abraham is a prophet who will pray for Abimelech. The common Hebrew word for 'prayer', tephillah, comes from this root.

G4100.use: Used about 245 times in the New Testament, in 21 books — first in Matthew 8:13; most often in John (98), Acts (39) and Romans (21).
senses: To believe that something is true, or to believe what someone says.
To believe in or on someone, meaning personal trust and reliance, not just agreeing with facts.
Those who believe are called 'believers', as in Acts 2:44.
To entrust something to someone, or to be entrusted with something, as in Romans 3:2.
G4100.note: John's Gospel uses this verb about 98 times, more than any other book, yet never uses the noun 'faith' (pistis). In the Greek Old Testament it mainly translates the Hebrew aman.

H539.use: Used about 106 times in the Old Testament, in 24 books — first in Genesis 15:6; most often in Psalms (16), Isaiah (15) and Job (10).
senses: To support or hold up; as a noun, a foster-father, a nurse, or the pillars supporting a door.
To be made firm, established, lasting and sure.
To be reliable, faithful and trustworthy.
To stand firm, to trust, and to believe in someone.
H539.note: Its first use is Genesis 15:6, where Abraham 'believed the LORD, and he counted it to him for righteousness.' The word 'amen' comes from the same root.

G863.use: Used about 146 times in the New Testament, in 11 books — first in Matthew 3:15; most often in Matthew (47), Mark (36) and Luke (32).
senses: To send away or let go, including giving up one's spirit at death, as in Matthew 27:50.
To release someone from a debt, and especially to forgive sins, as in 1 John 1:9.
To leave behind, abandon or neglect, as in leaving 'your first love' in Revelation 2:4.
To let, allow or permit, as in 'Suffer it to be so now' in Matthew 3:15.
G863.note: The basic picture is letting something go from oneself, which explains how one verb covers forgiving, leaving and allowing. In Matthew 18:27 it is used of a master cancelling a servant's debt.

H5545.use: Used about 46 times in the Old Testament, in 13 books — first in Exodus 34:9; most often in Leviticus (10), Numbers (8) and Jeremiah (6).
senses: To forgive or pardon a wrong.
To be forgiven, a form used often in the sacrifice laws of Leviticus and Numbers.
The KJV also renders it 'spare', meaning to hold back deserved punishment.
H5545.note: In the Old Testament this verb is used only of God forgiving, never of people forgiving one another. Its first use is Moses' plea in Exodus 34:9: 'pardon our iniquity and our sin.'

G1325.use: Used about 417 times in the New Testament, in 22 books — first in Matthew 4:9; most often in John (77), Luke (60) and Revelation (58).
senses: To give, bestow or grant something to someone, as in John 3:16.
To hand over, deliver or entrust, as when the Father gives judgment to the Son in John 5:22.
To yield or produce, as seed yields fruit in Mark 4:8.
To give oneself, as Christ gave his life 'a ransom for many' in Mark 10:45.
G1325.note: It is one of the most common verbs in the New Testament, used over 400 times. Paul quotes Jesus' saying 'It is more blessed to give than to receive' with this word in Acts 20:35.

H5414.use: Used about 2011 times in the Old Testament, in 38 books — first in Genesis 1:17; most often in Ezekiel (208), Deuteronomy (176) and Genesis (150).
senses: To give, grant, pay, lend or hand over something to someone.
To put, set or place something, or to appoint someone to a role.
To make or turn something into something else.
To allow or let; and in the phrase 'who will give?' it expresses a wish meaning 'if only!'
H5414.note: Used over 2,000 times, it is one of the most common verbs in the Old Testament. Its first use is Genesis 1:17, where God 'set' the lights in the sky.

G2212.use: Used about 119 times in the New Testament, in 16 books — first in Matthew 2:13; most often in John (35), Luke (26) and Matthew (14).
senses: To look for someone or something, as in 'seek, and ye shall find' in Matthew 7:7.
To search out in thought, to inquire into, or to seek God, as in Acts 17:27.
To strive after or desire, as in 'seek ye first the kingdom of God' in Matthew 6:33.
To require or demand, as in 'the Jews require a sign' in 1 Corinthians 1:22.
G2212.note: It can also mean plotting against someone's life, as in its first use, Matthew 2:13, where Herod seeks the young child to destroy him. In the Greek Old Testament it mainly translates the Hebrew baqash.

H1875.use: Used about 164 times in the Old Testament, in 25 books — first in Genesis 9:5; most often in 2 Chronicles (30), Psalms (24) and Ezekiel (16).
senses: To resort to or frequent a place.
To consult or inquire of God, and to seek him in prayer and worship.
To seek with care, to study, or to follow with diligence.
To require or demand, especially the 'requiring' of blood, as in Genesis 9:5.
H1875.note: Second Chronicles uses it more than any other book, often asking whether a king 'sought the LORD.' The later Jewish word midrash, meaning study or interpretation of Scripture, comes from this root.

G154.use: Used about 70 times in the New Testament, in 11 books — first in Matthew 5:42; most often in Matthew (14), Luke (11) and John (11).
senses: To ask for something, to request it, as in 'Ask, and it shall be given you' in Matthew 7:7.
To ask God in prayer, as in James 1:5-6.
To beg, call for or demand, as the crowd asked for Barabbas in Matthew 27:20.
G154.note: Older scholars drew a sharp line between this word and erōtaō, another word for 'ask', but in New Testament times the two had become nearly interchangeable. In the Greek Old Testament it mainly translates the Hebrew sha'al.

H7592.use: Used about 171 times in the Old Testament, in 27 books — first in Genesis 24:47; most often in 1 Samuel (31), 1 Kings (15) and Judges (14).
senses: To ask, or to ask for something, sometimes as a favour or a loan.
To inquire or ask a question, including consulting God.
To beg.
To grant something on request, letting a person ask successfully.
H7592.note: King Saul's name comes from this verb and means 'asked for.' To 'ask about someone's peace' was a normal greeting, which is why the KJV sometimes renders it 'salute.'

G2925.use: Used about 9 times in the New Testament, in 4 books — first in Matthew 7:7; most often in Luke (4), Acts (2) and Matthew (2).
senses: To knock, especially at a door.
Used as a picture of persistent prayer: 'knock, and it shall be opened unto you' in Matthew 7:7.
Used of the Lord knocking and waiting to be let in, as in Revelation 3:20.
G2925.note: In Acts 12:13-16 Peter, freed from prison, keeps knocking at the door while the household cannot believe it is him. In the Greek Old Testament it translates the Hebrew dāphaq in Song of Solomon 5:2.

H1849.use: Used about 3 times in the Old Testament, in 3 books — first in Genesis 33:13; most often in Genesis (1), Song of Solomon (1) and Judges (1).
senses: To knock, as at a door.
To beat on something violently.
To drive or push hard, as in overdriving a flock.
H1849.note: It appears only three times: Jacob's flocks would die if driven hard (Genesis 33:13), men beating on a door (Judges 19:22), and the beloved knocking in Song of Solomon 5:2.

G190.use: Used about 91 times in the New Testament, in 7 books — first in Matthew 4:20; most often in Matthew (25), Mark (19) and John (19).
senses: To accompany or follow someone, as the crowds followed Jesus in Matthew 4:25.
To follow as a disciple, committing to a teacher's way, as in Matthew 9:9.
To 'come after' someone, as in taking up one's cross and following in Matthew 10:38.
G190.note: The word pictures being 'on the same road' as someone. Its first use, Matthew 4:20, is the fishermen leaving their nets to follow Jesus, and almost all its uses are in the Gospels.

H1980.use: Used about 1549 times in the Old Testament, in 37 books — first in Genesis 2:14; most often in 1 Samuel (138), Genesis (122) and 1 Kings (122).
senses: To go, come, walk, depart or journey.
To walk as a picture of how one lives or behaves.
To go after someone, that is, to follow them.
To lead, bring or carry someone or something along.
H1980.note: Used over 1,500 times, it is one of the most common verbs in the Old Testament. The later Jewish term halakhah, meaning the 'way to walk' or practical law, comes from this root.

G191.use: Used about 436 times in the New Testament, in 23 books — first in Matthew 2:3; most often in Acts (91), Matthew (66) and Luke (65).
senses: To hear: to take in sound with the ears, or simply to have the ability to hear.
To listen and pay attention, as in "He who has ears to hear, let him hear" (Matthew 11:15).
To hear something reported or taught, and so to learn or understand it.
Used of God hearing and answering prayer (1 John 5:14-15).
G191.note: In the Greek Old Testament this is the usual word for the Hebrew shama, "hear." English "acoustic" comes from the same Greek root.

H8085.use: Used about 1160 times in the Old Testament, in 39 books — first in Genesis 3:8; most often in Jeremiah (184), Isaiah (106) and Deuteronomy (92).
senses: To hear with the ears, or to hear news about someone or something.
To listen closely and take to heart, often meaning to agree to a request or give heed.
Very often it means to obey: to hear a command and act on it.
In a causing sense it means to make others hear: to announce, proclaim or sound aloud.
H8085.note: This verb opens Deuteronomy 6:4, "Hear, O Israel," and that verse is still called the Shema after its first word. Hebrew has no separate common word for "obey"; this verb covers both hearing and obeying.

G3421.use: Used about 21 times in the New Testament, in 13 books — first in Matthew 16:9; most often in Hebrews (3), Revelation (3) and John (3).
senses: To call something to mind and remember it, such as people, words or past events.
To keep someone in mind with care, as Paul asks, "Remember my bonds" (Colossians 4:18).
To make mention of or speak about something, as in Hebrews 11:22.
G3421.note: It comes from a word meaning "mindful." Jesus' shortest warning uses it: "Remember Lot's wife" (Luke 17:32).

H2142.use: Used about 232 times in the Old Testament, in 32 books — first in Genesis 8:1; most often in Psalms (53), Isaiah (26) and Ezekiel (21).
senses: To remember: to recall or call something to mind.
To be remembered or thought of, to be brought back to someone's mind.
To remind others, or to keep something in remembrance by mentioning or recording it.
To make a memorial, so that something is not forgotten.
H2142.note: Its first use is Genesis 8:1, "God remembered Noah," and the verse goes straight on to God sending a wind to dry the waters. In Hebrew, remembering is often the first step toward acting.

G1586.use: Used about 22 times in the New Testament, in 7 books — first in Mark 13:20; most often in Acts (7), John (5) and Luke (4).
senses: To pick out or choose something for oneself, such as a place at table (Luke 14:7).
Used of people choosing others for a task, like the church choosing the seven in Acts 6:5.
Used of Jesus choosing his disciples (John 15:16).
Used of God's own choosing of people and things (Ephesians 1:4).
G1586.note: It is built from ek ("out of") and legō, whose older meaning is "to gather or pick," giving the picture of picking out. In the Greek Old Testament it mostly translates the Hebrew bachar, "choose."

H977.use: Used about 171 times in the Old Testament, in 22 books — first in Genesis 6:2; most often in Deuteronomy (31), Isaiah (20) and 2 Chronicles (16).
senses: To choose, select or decide for one thing over another.
Used of God choosing a people, a place or a person for himself.
To be chosen or selected, as what is choice and excellent.
H977.note: Strong's notes that its root idea is to test or try, and so to select what proves best. Deuteronomy repeatedly speaks of "the place the LORD your God will choose" (Deuteronomy 12:5).

G5091.use: Used about 21 times in the New Testament, in 8 books — first in Matthew 15:4; most often in Matthew (6), John (6) and Mark (3).
senses: To set a value or price on something; used of the price set on Jesus (Matthew 27:9).
To honour: to show respect and value to a person.
Used in the command to honour father and mother (Matthew 15:4).
Used of honouring God and the Son (John 5:23).
G5091.note: The same root covers both "price" and "honour": to honour someone is to treat them as valuable. In the Greek Old Testament it often translates the Hebrew kabad.

H3513.use: Used about 113 times in the Old Testament, in 26 books — first in Genesis 18:20; most often in Isaiah (20), Psalms (11) and 1 Samuel (11).
senses: To be heavy or weighty, in a good sense: rich, honoured or glorious.
To honour or glorify someone, to give them weight and respect.
In a bad sense: to be burdensome, severe or grievous.
To be dull or unresponsive, like heavy ears, dim eyes or a hardened heart.
H3513.note: The picture behind it is weight. The same verb is used for honouring father and mother (Exodus 20:12) and for Pharaoh's heart being made heavy, or hardened (Exodus 8:15).

G837.use: Used about 23 times in the New Testament, in 11 books — first in Matthew 6:28; most often in Acts (4), Luke (4) and Colossians (3).
senses: To grow or increase, used of plants, children and growing crowds.
To cause to grow, as when "God gave the growth" (1 Corinthians 3:6).
Used of the spread of the gospel: "the word of God grew" (Acts 12:24).
Used of growing in grace and knowledge of God (2 Peter 3:18).
G837.note: John the Baptist uses it in John 3:30: "He must increase, but I must decrease."

H1431.use: Used about 117 times in the Old Testament, in 31 books — first in Genesis 12:2; most often in Psalms (16), Genesis (14) and Isaiah (9).
senses: To grow up, as a child does, or to become large.
To become great or important, or to make someone great and powerful.
To magnify or praise, declaring how great someone is.
In a bad sense, to make oneself great: to boast or act proudly.
H1431.note: Its first use is God's promise to Abram, "I will make your name great" (Genesis 12:2). The call "O magnify the LORD with me" in Psalm 34:3 uses the same verb.

G4863.use: Used about 61 times in the New Testament, in 7 books — first in Matthew 2:4; most often in Matthew (24), Acts (11) and John (8).
senses: To gather or bring things together, like grain into a barn or leftover food (John 6:12).
To call people together, or for people to come together, especially for a meeting.
To welcome someone in as a guest: "I was a stranger and you took me in" (Matthew 25:35).
G4863.note: It literally means "to lead together." Its noun form, synagōgē, is where the English word "synagogue" comes from.

H6908.use: Used about 127 times in the Old Testament, in 25 books — first in Genesis 41:35; most often in Isaiah (20), Ezekiel (16) and 2 Chronicles (11).
senses: To gather or collect things, such as grain stored up in Egypt (Genesis 41:35).
To assemble people, or for people to gather together.
Often used of God gathering his scattered people back from the nations.
H6908.note: Prophets such as Isaiah and Ezekiel use it often for the promised regathering of Israel. The modern Hebrew word "kibbutz" comes from the same root.

G1209.use: Used about 57 times in the New Testament, in 15 books — first in Matthew 10:14; most often in Luke (16), Matthew (10) and Acts (8).
senses: To take or accept what is offered, such as a cup or a letter.
To accept a message in one's mind, such as receiving the word of God (1 Thessalonians 2:13).
To welcome a person kindly as a guest (Matthew 10:40).
To take into one's arms, as Simeon took the infant Jesus (Luke 2:28).
G1209.note: Stephen's dying prayer uses it: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" (Acts 7:59).

H7521.use: Used about 56 times in the Old Testament, in 20 books — first in Genesis 33:10; most often in Psalms (13), Leviticus (11) and Job (4).
senses: To be pleased with someone, to look on them with favour.
To accept favourably, often used of God accepting an offering or a person.
To make oneself pleasing, or to seek someone's favour.
To pay off or make up what is owed, as the land making up its missed sabbaths.
H7521.note: Leviticus uses it for offerings being accepted by God. In Leviticus 26:34 it describes the land "enjoying," or making up, its sabbath rests.

G1720.use: Used about 1 times in the New Testament, in 1 book — first in John 20:22; most often in John (1).
senses: To breathe on or blow upon someone.
Used only once in the New Testament, when the risen Jesus breathed on his disciples (John 20:22).
G1720.note: The Greek Old Testament uses this same verb in Genesis 2:7, where God breathed into the man's nostrils the breath of life.

H5397.use: Used about 24 times in the Old Testament, in 10 books — first in Genesis 2:7; most often in Job (7), Isaiah (4) and Joshua (3).
senses: Breath, especially the breath of life in people and creatures.
The breath of God, which gives life or blows as a blast of his power.
Every breathing thing, meaning all living creatures.
The inner spirit of a person.
H5397.note: Its first use is Genesis 2:7, where God breathes into the man "the breath of life." Proverbs 20:27 calls the human spirit (this word) "the lamp of the LORD."

H8055.use: Used about 155 times in the Old Testament, in 30 books — first in Exodus 4:14; most often in Psalms (52), Proverbs (17) and Deuteronomy (10).
senses: To rejoice or be glad.
To rejoice in worship, celebrating before God.
In a bad sense, to gloat or exult over someone's trouble.
To make others glad or cause them to rejoice.
H8055.note: Strong's suggests the root idea is to brighten up. Its first use is Exodus 4:14, where Aaron will be "glad in his heart" to see Moses.

G2198.use: Used about 143 times in the New Testament, in 20 books — first in Matthew 4:4; most often in Romans (23), John (18) and Revelation (14).
senses: To be alive, physically living, as opposed to being dead.
Used of God as "the living God" (Matthew 16:16), and of coming back to life.
To live one's life in a certain way, such as "by faith" or "to God."
Used in pictures like "living water," meaning fresh flowing water (John 4:10).
G2198.note: "Living water" was the ordinary term for running spring water, as opposed to still water in a cistern. The oath "as I live" (Romans 14:11) echoes a common Old Testament oath.

H2421.use: Used about 282 times in the Old Testament, in 27 books — first in Genesis 3:22; most often in Genesis (59), Ezekiel (48) and Psalms (31).
senses: To live, to have life, or to stay alive.
To revive or recover, from sickness, discouragement or even death.
To keep someone alive or let them live.
To give life, restore or refresh.
H2421.note: Eve's name is linked with life, "the mother of all living" (Genesis 3:20). In Ezekiel 37:3 God asks, "Can these bones live?" using this verb.

G103.use: Used about 5 times in the New Testament, in 3 books — first in Ephesians 5:19; most often in Revelation (3), Ephesians (1) and Colossians (1).
senses: To sing, especially songs of praise to God (Ephesians 5:19).
To sing a song, as the heavenly crowds sing a "new song" (Revelation 5:9).
G103.note: The related noun ōdē is the source of the English word "ode." In the Greek Old Testament this verb mostly translates the Hebrew shir, "sing."

H7891.use: Used about 87 times in the Old Testament, in 18 books — first in Exodus 15:1; most often in Psalms (27), Nehemiah (17) and 2 Chronicles (9).
senses: To sing.
As a noun-like form, a singer, male or female, such as the temple singers.
To be sung, of a song being sung.
H7891.note: Its first use is Exodus 15:1, when Moses and Israel sang after crossing the Red Sea. The book called the Song of Songs takes its name from the related noun.

G1070.use: Used about 2 times in the New Testament, in 1 book — first in Luke 6:21; most often in Luke (2).
senses: To laugh, as a sign of joy or satisfaction.
Jesus uses it both as a promise and a warning in Luke 6:21 and 6:25.
G1070.note: It appears only twice, both in Luke's Sermon on the Plain: "Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh," and "Woe to you who laugh now."

H6711.use: Used about 13 times in the Old Testament, in 3 books — first in Genesis 17:17; most often in Genesis (11), Exodus (1) and Judges (1).
senses: To laugh, whether in joy, surprise or disbelief.
To mock or make fun of someone.
To play, jest or make sport, sometimes of play between husband and wife (Genesis 26:8).
H6711.note: Isaac's name comes from this verb. Both Abraham (Genesis 17:17) and Sarah (Genesis 18:12) laughed at the promise of his birth.
